newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FORECAST--Australian CPI to fall to four year low.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST--Australian CPI to fall to four year low.

text.p: Australia's inflation rate fell to its lowest level in four years during the March quarter, economists expect data due on Wednesday to show, offering some hope to those holding out for another rate cut.
More likely, however, is that data will add to the case that there is no need for a near term rate rise, analysts said.

With the impact of the three cuts in official rates last year, and a further round of mortgage rate cuts earlier this year still flowing through to the Consumer Price Index (CPI), some economists forecast negative inflation in the quarter.
The key underlying inflation measure is also expected to remain at the low end of the Reserve Bank's (RBA) target band.
"We expect both the headline and underlying rates to confirm low and stable inflation -- but have no immediate implications for monetary policy," Macquarie Bank economists said.
The median forecast of the 29 economists surveyed by Reuters was for a first quarter CPI rise of 0.1 percent, the smallest quarterly increase since September 1992.
In annual terms this would leave the CPI 1.2 percent higher over the year, the lowest annual rate since March 1993.
Quarterly forecasts ranged from a 0.1 percent fall to a 0.3 percent rise. In the December quarter, the CPI rose 0.2 percent for an annual increase of 1.5 percent.

Underlying inflation is expected to have risen 0.4 percent in the quarter to be 2.1 percent higher over the year, matching its December quarter levels. Quarterly forecasts range from a 0.2 percent rise to a 0.5 percent rise.
The RBA aims to keep the underlying rate to an average of between two and three percent over a number of years.

The underlying rate is expected to be at the low end of the target band in 1997, as analysts said despite some volatility against the U.S. dollar since last December, the Australian dollar has held up well in trade weighted terms, and partial indicators are showing little evidence of price pressures.
Underlying inflation strips out the more volatile components of the CPI, aiming to present a more accurate picture of supply and demand forces in the economy.

As such it is more steady than the CPI -- in the two years to December 1996 annual CPI ranged from 1.5 to 5.1 percent, while the underlying rate ranged between 1.9 and 3.3 percent. The inflation data will follow an expected inflation-friendly outcome to the union movement's "living wage" claim on Tuesday, and further gains are seen on the inflation front in 1997.

The low inflation outlook, combined with some softness in recent economic data which has raised some doubts over the robustness of the economy in early 1997, is expected to keep talk of another rate around in the marketplace, analysts said,

"Markets will start taking seriously the possibility of another rate cut if the wage and inflation figures do exceed expectations -- after all, what use is zero inflation if the unemployment rate is heading back above nine percent," Colonial State Bank economist Hans Kunnen said.

However, the prospect of another rate cut, despite the favourable inflation outlook, is still seen as quite slim. The median forecast of economists surveyed by Reuters was that there was a 25 percent chance of another rate cut, with a highest forecast of a 50 percent chance.

"Our view remains that the growth prospects for Australia are good and we think the market will refocus on this following the release of what we are forecasting to be very bullish first quarter inflation and wages data," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economists said in a commentary.

But while economists do not generally see a rate cut as likely, they said Wednesday's data, and Tuesday's wage case decision, should provide evidence that rates will not be edging higher in the near term.
